q: When you look at the international events beforehand, when you look at the national events, sporting events, that was sort of the logical time.
c: Announcing the 7 November election date at National's caucus retreat in Christchurch.

q: We've been doing a big turnaround, we've been fixing a lot of the basics. We now have an opportunity, as this recovery comes through, not just to watch it come through but to actually shape the future of this country...
c: Election-date announcement; pitching National's economic record.

q: There was a confidence vote in my leadership this morning at our caucus meeting, and I have the full support of our caucus. And our caucus is united, and it is determined to win this election.
c: After surviving a second caucus confidence vote in four months, triggered by Chris Penk's challenge.

q: Chris Penk launched a leadership challenge this week, which resulted in today's confidence vote. This makes his role untenable, and as such I have removed his portfolios.
c: Statement removing Chris Penk's ministerial portfolios.

q: I just wrapped up my campaign launch speech, and my message was simple: Where do you want your hard-earned money going, to you and your family, or to Labour and their mates? Party Vote National for no new taxes.
c: X post after National's campaign launch at the Auckland Convention Centre.

q: It's absolute madness.
c: On RNZ Morning Report, responding to NZ First's policy of buying back BNZ (said 'that's just not going to happen').

q: He can't find a pathway to get into government without those four radical parties and six leaders, that's going to be chaos.
c: On Chris Hipkins' likely coalition partners (Greens, Te Pāti Māori, Opportunity), RNZ Morning Report.

q: We want to work with parties that want no new taxes. It's as simple as that.
c: Holding to his rule-out of working with the Opportunity Party, citing its land value tax.

q: If you can work, you should. Welfare should be firm, fair and affordable. A safety net for Kiwis who need it, not a system that gets abused at taxpayers' expense.
c: X post announcing National's Jobseeker changes, including random drug testing (posted 8 Oct NZT).

q: I have the support of my caucus as their leader. Caucus has answered clearly and decisively. It has backed my leadership, and that matter is now closed.
c: After forcing a caucus confidence vote on his own leadership amid media reports of discontent.

q: Kiwis expect the media to ask us the tough questions about our policies... They are not interested in the media soap opera.
c: Same statement after the April confidence vote.

q: New Zealand is digging its way out of the post-Covid hole.
c: Delivering Budget 2026.

q: Kiwis can look forward with confidence, they just need to choose it, they just need to vote for it.
c: Closing line of her Budget 2026 speech.

q: It's a Budget that does what's right for the country... this is not a time to be getting us further into the hock, to be whacking another set of bills on the credit card.
c: RNZ Morning Report, asked whether a restrained Budget was risky in election year.

q: I will go to the campaign trail as the National Party finance spokesperson with my view on what would be appropriate, well signalled, fair, transparent, gradual, gradual changes to New Zealand superannuation.
c: Post-Budget, on NZ Super costs rising; she added: "I haven't been able to convince my coalition partners yet, but I retain hope."

q: One for all, all for one. And when the caucus, by majority, have confidence in the leader, then we all stand together, backing the leader.
c: As deputy leader, after Luxon survived the April caucus confidence vote.

q: This is the least credible fiscal plan released by a major party in living memory.
c: National press release titled 'Labour's fiscal plan a fraud'. Labour says its plan is fully costed and funded.

q: I think what the Prime Minister was saying, which I would broadly agree with, is that the country has very difficult challenges ahead of it and we should spend our time focused on those challenges.
c: After voting in support of Luxon in the April caucus confidence vote; he described the caucus discussion as "good, honest and robust".

q: Today is a major milestone. After 35 years of the RMA, Parliament has passed legislation for a fundamentally different way of planning for New Zealand's future.
c: Press release as the Planning Bill and Natural Environment Bill (RMA replacement) passed third reading.

q: Passing these Bills is not the end of the job. The next task is making sure the new system works in practice.
c: Same release; the full new system is intended to operate by 2030.

q: I will consider the reforms to have failed.
c: Newsroom interview: if, in five years, the new planning system has not made the fast-track regime unnecessary.

q: With this reshuffle, I'm pleased to be taking on the role of Energy Minister and to have been appointed campaign chair for the National Party.
c: Statement after Luxon's April reshuffle, which moved the campaign-chair role from Chris Bishop to Brown.

q: Kiwis remember what life was like under Labour – inflation peaking, crime soaring, and public services like health and education going backwards.
c: LinkedIn post on becoming campaign chair.

q: The Advertising Standards Authority has not said KiwiSaver wouldn't be affected by Labour's capital gains tax - it has only suggested that KiwiSaver may not be impacted to the same extent as rental properties, baches and businesses.
c: Responding after the ASA partly upheld a complaint that a National attack ad on Labour's CGT was misleading.

q: This qualification rewards hard work and is designed to encourage young people to strive to do their very best, and ultimately to feel proud of what they achieved.
c: Confirming details of the qualification replacing NCEA (NZCE at Year 12, NZACE at Year 13).

q: We want young people leaving school with qualifications that are clear, rigorous and widely understood by parents, employers, tertiary providers and students themselves.
c: National Party release on the NCEA replacement.

q: I didn't challenge for the leadership.
c: First media appearance after the failed Penk leadership challenge, amid speculation she was the alternative leader.

q: I want to be the minister of Education and Immigration - mostly education - for the next nine years. I love my job, and I've got so much more to do.
c: Same appearance, ruling herself out of leadership ambitions.

q: I didn't do any numbers at all. I can categorically tell you, I don't know if anyone did do any numbers. I certainly didn't.
c: Denying she counted caucus votes for Chris Penk's challenge.

q: This is about no new taxes, and I can't be clearer, this is the fundamental choice of this election.
c: Upgrading National's pledge from 'no new taxes on working people' to 'no new taxes', ruling out a bed tax and bank tax.

q: We've got to make sure the banks are taxed fairly... As a minister in this Government, I am still actively considering the taxation of banks and what that looks like.
c: May 2026 comments (exact day not given in source), as quoted by 1News when she later dropped the idea.

q: I have looked at what the banks are being taxed at now and measures for changing that, and there are no other measures that I can see won't result in additional costs for Kiwis.
c: Explaining why National dropped a bank tax under its 'no new taxes' pledge.

q: These changes are about ensuring treatments are safe and carefully managed, while maintaining access to care for those who need it.
c: As Health Minister, announcing a pause on new puberty-blocker prescriptions for gender dysphoria pending a UK trial.

q: I'm focused on making sure that we win in November and making sure that we deliver a National-led government.
c: On taking over as campaign chair; asked his experience, he replied "winning elections".

q: I have never been part of a conversation where that has been said to our prime minister.
c: Asked repeatedly whether he had been in a conversation telling Luxon he was losing caucus support.

q: Obviously I love being the campaign chair, and it's a role I enjoy doing, but it's fine - I've got plenty of things to do.
c: After losing the campaign-chair and Leader of the House roles in the April reshuffle while becoming Attorney-General.

q: Here's what is exempt from our simple, targeted capital gains tax: the family home, farms, inheritances, KiwiSaver, shares, businesses, and personal items.
c: X post defending Labour's proposed capital gains tax on property.

q: #BREAKING: Labour will provide three free doctor's visits a year for everyone, delivered via a brand new Medicard and funded by a targeted tax on property profits, excluding the family home.
c: X post announcing Labour's flagship health/tax policy.

q: We want to send a really clear message that... you can work constructively with people, still have disagreements, without getting into abuse.
c: RNZ Morning Report, ahead of the joint Labour–Greens press conference at Waitangi.

q: They're in court. That's really where their focus should be.
c: On Te Pāti Māori, which was in the High Court over the expulsion of MP Mariameno Kapa-Kingi.

q: Backstabbing and infighting just means more delay and more distraction for New Zealand. If National can't govern itself, how can New Zealanders trust it to govern the country?
c: Media release after Luxon survived the Penk leadership challenge.

q: This election is about the cost of living. This election is about your cost of living.
c: Opening of his campaign launch speech in Manukau.

q: Christopher Luxon promised to fix the cost of living. He's had three years. He's failed.
c: Campaign launch speech; he also called National's claims about Labour's tax policy "bullshit".

q: Neo-liberal, trickledown economics does not work.
c: Campaign launch, announcing a 10% write-off of eligible student loan balances.

q: We're talking about seamless travel between Pacific countries and New Zealand … and a recognition of the cost and burden that the current system puts on New Zealand Pacific families.
c: Announcing Labour's pledge to extend visa-waiver travel to Pacific Islands Forum citizens.

q: Our relationship has matured enough for us to be able to move to a place that they have access to the same electronic system that 60 other countries have. It's the right thing to do.
c: Same announcement.

q: The expectation is that the rules still apply … and our expectation is that people will follow them.
c: Responding to concerns about rising overstayer rates.

q: We get about 3.1% on average over the forecast period. So we believe the 3% is conservative, and we think is prudent given that the forecasts do change...
c: interest.co.nz interview defending the house-price growth assumption behind Labour's CGT revenue.

q: I don't want it going heaps over or heaps under. For me, [it] is just making sure there is... steady and stable house prices.
c: Same interview, asked what Labour wants for house prices.

q: Tax cuts need to be allowed as the fiscal and economic environment allows for it.
c: Same interview, on whether income-tax changes are possible once in surplus.

q: I'm not a fool in terms of how hard it is to knock out incumbents.
c: RNZ interview on Labour's chances of winning all seven Māori electorates.

q: You can buy into that strategy if every everything's working well, but they're not even voting for themselves.
c: Criticising Te Pāti Māori's electorate-vote-only strategy, which he warned could invite a backlash against the Māori seats.

q: We weren't talking about voting for an overhang. We weren't talking about voting for people who had different politics from us, all we were talking about was using the system to get more Māori through Labour into the Parliament.
c: Responding to Debbie Ngarewa-Packer's charge that Labour used a similar strategy in 2017.

q: Nobody believes her. No one who is aware of the situation, who followed the situation, believes her.
c: On Erica Stanford's denial of involvement in the National leadership challenge.

q: Solar is the future and an important part of our energy security, so anything that makes it easier and cheaper to install is welcome.
c: Labour release responding to National's home-energy loans policy.

q: Labour has and will always back renewable energy while National has spent three years making New Zealand's energy problems worse.
c: Same release.

q: There's nothing complicated about these costings.
c: Launching Labour's $160m SolarSaver policy; asked if confident in the costings she said "we have our numbers right".

q: We don't have enough of the plug-in systems because they're illegal in New Zealand at the moment - the first step is making them legal.
c: Same launch, on plug-in solar for renters.

q: It's not nice, and it's hard when you have to explain it to your kids, but it's even worse for the people that are actually living as homeless people, because they have nowhere to lay down with a roof over their heads at night time.
c: First-reading debate on the move-on orders bill, which she called "purely ideological".

q: People aren't dumb. They know that while their cost of living has gone through the roof, corporate profits have skyrocketed and the wealthiest 150 rich listers now own more than half of the country.
c: Launching the Greens' tax package (wealth, inheritance and corporate taxes; income-tax cuts for 96%).

q: Someone would have to pay their taxes fairly. That is the case with all New Zealanders who have income taxes that they have to pay.
c: 1News Breakfast, asked whether someone could be forced to sell an inherited asset to pay the proposed inheritance tax.

q: Congratulations, they are incredibly lucky to be an individual that is inheriting an excess of $2 million.
c: Same interview, on a hypothetical heir to a $2m investment property.

q: We must electrify everything we can. We need homegrown, sustainable resilience in our energy system, powering everything we do.
c: Greens' State of the Planet address calling for a National Electrification Plan during the fuel crisis.

q: No-one is hoarding, attacking, or starting wars over sun, wind, water and geothermal energy. They don't come through the Strait of Hormuz.
c: Same address.

q: The polls are going to continue to bounce around at the margins over the next few weeks, and this is why it's really important to understand that nothing is set in stone.
c: Reacting to a 1News–Verian poll with the Greens on 16%; she said the Greens would "very clearly" work with Labour.

q: What is happening in the Middle East is, first and foremost, a human catastrophe. Civilians are being killed and injured, livelihoods are being destroyed, international law is being broken.
c: State of the Planet address, on the 2026 Iran war.

q: The cost of food, of energy, of rent keeps climbing, while wages stay flat. Communities that were already struggling are being hit hardest by rising price, by wars they did not start...
c: Same address.

q: We believe in building an international rules-based order that protects the environment, upholds human rights and supports enduring peace-building work.
c: Same address, on foreign policy.

q: Essential services like healthcare, education, and infrastructure could be funded if the super-rich and mega-corporates like the supermarkets duopoly, banks, and power companies contribute fairly to the society they profit from.
c: Greens' tax package launch.

q: We need to get big money out of politics. The donation should only be by people, not by company.
c: Pacific Media Network interview on the Greens' $30,000 donation-cap policy.

q: Here we have the US trying to find a way to get into the Cook Islands, but is this heading towards a military base? That would be something that I would not be in favour of.
c: Same interview, on Pacific security.

q: We don't need more militarisation of the Pacific, for the Pacific to become a more contested space.
c: Same interview.

q: Individuals will still have the right to opt out if they choose to. The only difference is that workers would be opting out rather than opting in. The default should be that workers are represented and backed, not the other way around.
c: Green release on his member's bill to make union membership the default for new employees.

q: If they comply and go home, they're not going to be charged. The minister realises they don't have a home, right? Where exactly are they supposed to move on? Should they go to your house?
c: First-reading debate on the move-on orders bill.

q: Where exactly are these kids meant to go? Would you like them to go sleep in a bush? Would you like them to go sleep under a bridge?
c: Same debate, objecting that the orders (as introduced) applied to people as young as 14. The final law applies to those 18 and over.

q: This is the worst homelessness in our history, with 57,000 women homeless and half of all homeless people under the age of 24. The Government's response has been a drop in the bucket to meaningfully address this crisis.
c: Green release as housing spokesperson.

q: Restoring commuter rail will give smaller regions and towns the benefits of more travellers stopping at their town stations, creating more economic opportunities and connecting them to main centres and other towns.
c: Announcing the Greens' $4b intercity passenger-rail plan as transport spokesperson.

q: The train journey from Auckland to Wellington is long, which makes it perfect for an overnight service. All that is needed is new, comfortable sleeper trains and operating funding.
c: Same announcement.

q: Years of underinvestment in public transport have left our cities harder to get around without a car.
c: Announcing free public transport for children, students and others and a $2 adult fare.

q: Since the signing of He Whakaputanga me Te Tiriti, tangata whenua rights and the wellbeing of our communities have been attacked, our focus must remain on the kaupapa: tino rangatiratanga.
c: Statement on standing for the Greens in Te Tai Tokerau.

q: For decades, the Green Party has stood alongside iwi hapū on the ground fighting for te taiao, the right to accessible health care and ending houselesness, and upholding tino rangatiratanga.
c: Same statement.

q: A vote for Hūhana Lyndon in Te Tai Tokerau and a Party Vote Green is a vote for strong Māori representation, thriving communities and a future that works for all of us in the north.
c: Her 2026 Green Party candidate page, which also pledges to "Revoke Fast Track Projects". (Page undated.)

q: In my experience, voters are often busy, but they're not stupid, and it's never wise to talk down to them.
c: Responding to Luxon calling strategic vote-splitting "insanely stupid"; he said "both votes belong to the voter".

q: ACT will finish the settlements and wind up the Waitangi Tribunal. The Waitangi Tribunal has been part of New Zealand's constitutional landscape for more than fifty years. It has made an important contribution, particularly in helping address historical grievances.
c: X post announcing ACT's policy to dissolve the Tribunal once historical claims are settled (post continues).

q: If someone wants to decide how ratepayer money is spent, they can run for council in an election like anyone else.
c: X post after Parliament passed a law ending voting rights for unelected members of council committees.

q: If you're on a benefit you have an obligation to those paying taxes to fund it. You must be work ready, like they are. Many New Zealanders face random drug testing as a condition of work, so should the beneficiaries they fund.
c: X post backing drug testing of beneficiaries after National's welfare policy release.

q: National's energy policy has near perfect overlap with ours released last week. It bodes well for a re-elected coalition acting together to make energy abundant and affordable.
c: X post on National's energy plan.

q: Labour's promise to forgive 10 per cent of student loan debt will sound attractive to loan holders at first, but it is an accounting switch that should be attractive to nobody.
c: X post responding to Labour's campaign-launch student-loan policy.

q: Judges keep using their leeway to give burglars more chances, and the burglars keep reoffending.
c: Announcing ACT's policy to add burglary to a Three Strikes regime (minimum three years' prison on a third strike).

q: Imprisoning repeat burglars will protect New Zealanders from a small group of offenders who have shown, time after time, that they have no respect for other people's homes or property. They will not be able to victimise us from a jail cell.
c: Same announcement.

q: When someone does the right thing, gets up and goes to work to unlock their own potential, they shouldn't have to worry about some deadbeat invading their home and taking their hard-earned property.
c: Same announcement.

q: It's a campaign election policy but I would feel that our coalition would get in behind this because they have gotten behind ACT's ideas throughout this term of government.
c: Saying there was "no need" to consult coalition partners first.

q: While discussions are ongoing, Cabinet has not agreed any final decisions.
c: On the coalition's stalled pledge to reverse the live-animal-export ban, which he said he could not get Cabinet agreement on this term.

q: New Zealand's farms, orchards, and fishing fleets generate $60 billion in exports every year. Right now, they can't find enough capable workers to do the job, held back by a chronic labour shortage that the current immigration system simply isn't equipped to solve.
c: Announcing ACT's Rural Workforce Visa at Fieldays.

q: Farmers deserve a massive thank you. While politicians in Wellington talk about prosperity, rural New Zealand goes out and earns it.
c: ACT release on record forecast primary-sector exports ($64.3b).

q: Punishing them with ideological targets while overseas competitors produce food less efficiently is bad for farmers, bad for consumers, and bad for the climate.
c: Same release, on ACT's 'science-based' (split-gas) climate approach for agriculture.

q: Let's be honest, there are a lot of little shits in classrooms, and we need to address that if we're going to lift education standards.
c: Announcing ACT's policy to let teachers remove disruptive students and use 'reasonable force'. Labour's education spokesperson called the language unacceptable.

q: We can't have the situation where that line is blurred. This has nothing to do with corporal punishment. This has nothing to do with punishing the child who is the problem.
c: Same announcement.

q: The ambiguity that exists at the moment means many teachers just can't even face the prospect of doing it.
c: Same announcement, on current guidance for physical restraint.

q: The Working with Children Card would give parents confidence that their children are in safe hands.
c: Announcing ACT's proposed continuous-vetting card as children's spokesperson.

q: The system ensures that cardholders are safe the whole time they work with children, not just up until a check was last completed.
c: Same announcement.

q: Nobody should have to stay in a violent home because they're worried about what will happen to their pet.
c: Announcing ACT's policy to criminalise using pets to coerce family-violence victims.

q: Family violence isn't just about physical abuse. Perpetrators use threats against beloved pets as another way to intimidate and trap their victims.
c: Same announcement.

q: It was their deal, the ACT Party's deal with the National Party. We were opposed to this from the word go but you've only got so many cards you can play.
c: Vowing to repeal the Regulatory Standards Act a week after all eight NZ First MPs voted for its third reading.

q: After days of speculation and distraction it has boiled down to 'much ado about nothing'.
c: On Luxon surviving the Penk leadership challenge.

q: New Zealand First will substantially reduce non-essential immigration and restore the principle that immigration is a privilege, not a right.
c: Unveiling NZ First's immigration platform, including a referendum on capping resident visas at 20,000 a year.

q: We need immigration to New Zealand. We always have. It has been an essential part of our history...
c: Same announcement.

q: The Treaty of Waitangi Tribunal has become a make-work organisation – now hearing any and all claims that in a former time would've been dismissed on application as being inappropriate.
c: X post after announcing NZ First would abolish the Waitangi Tribunal within 100 days of the next government.

q: The Opportunist Party "bottom lines" are more like a "wrinkly derrière".
c: X post responding to the Opportunity Party's five non-negotiable policies.

q: We need to double the size of the economy and we cannot do that if we neglect the very markets we need to be in.
c: X post criticising National's plan to cut aid outside the Pacific to fund health spending.

q: They're the mainstream media's party, and you guys are no good at politics.
c: Predicting the Opportunity Party would fall short of 5%, after a 1News–Verian poll put it on 7%.

q: My honest view, and I have to be bound by the collective decision, I always wanted ministers to be making the decisions.
c: Announcing NZ First would campaign on giving ministers the final say on fast-track approvals.

q: I just can't get my head around why four individuals...[are] more morally fit to make those calls than politicians and I'm going to campaign on that.
c: Same event, on expert panels deciding fast-track applications.

q: When the government was formed in 2023, the Prime Minister met with Winston and myself. I kinda got hōhā and went for a holiday to the Gold Coast so if there's anything wrong with the coalition agreement you might want to blame me.
c: Joking remark at the same event.

q: Providing they're not breaking the law, I feel that they should make the most of the opportunity. I don't feel that I'm being reckless.
c: As Resources Minister, urging mining companies to "get your applications in ASAP" for fast-track before the election.

q: Seniors need more choice and more security. New Zealand First will deliver legislation that protects residents where needed, supports more housing options, and recognises the sector's role in aged care.
c: On the Retirement Villages Amendment Bill being deferred to next term.

q: Three-month buy-backs are political posturing. They would damage the sector and make residents more vulnerable.
c: Same release, rejecting Labour's policy that villages repay departing residents within three months.

q: I'm considering a review of the excise, and that's what we took forward to cabinet, that it's time that we started to consider a review on how our excise structure is for all of these products.
c: As Associate Health Minister (tobacco); health experts raised concerns, and she said she did not intend to reduce tobacco tax.

q: I want to see policies in place that stop people smoking and stop the supply of illicit cigarettes and tobacco.
c: Same interview.

q: The water storage project [will] help unlock economic potential – boost food production and create jobs.
c: As Associate Regional Development Minister, announcing an $18.13m Regional Infrastructure Fund loan for the Tukituki water project.

q: As a key food-producing region, Hawke's Bay has the potential for expansion with reliable long-term water supplies.
c: Same announcement.

q: National adopted most of our other policies so there's still hope.
c: Federated Farmers rural debate, asked why NZ First backs its 'Use It or Lose It' Fonterra milk-access policy when no other party does.

q: New Zealand First has consistently advocated for national sovereignty, the protection of democratic institutions, and policies that put New Zealanders first.
c: NewZeal release announcing he would stand for NZ First.

q: My values remain unchanged... This is not a departure from those convictions, it is an transition in how they maybe carried forward.
c: Same release (wording as published).

q: One of the things about a bigger party is that sometimes they use this phrase, 'We're a broad church'. When you try to be all things to all people, you tend to at times compromise on the big issues.
c: 1News interview on why he chose NZ First rather than returning to National.

q: We had people giving us confidence, but not enough to get us over the threshold.
c: Same interview, on NewZeal's 2023 result; asked if the switch was pragmatism he said "realism too".

q: There's one plan, two votes; our plan has to be to focus on the candidate votes. We trust you with the party vote we trust and we see your love for our people, for our taiao. We trust that you will choose what is right.
c: Speech at Te Pāti Māori campaign launch, Te Poho o Rāwiri Marae, Gisborne

q: You have the power to bring this government to its knees.
c: Campaign launch speech, Gisborne

q: It's our whānau on the ground. It's not the corporate exploiters, it's not the Federated Farmers, it's not the Fonterras, it's not the BPs, it's not all the mates they're bending to - it's you.
c: Campaign launch speech, Gisborne

q: We said this election is bigger than any one party. Our list reflects that commitment.
c: On the party's one-person list

q: Even under fast-track legislation designed to push projects through, seabed mining has been found to cause unacceptable harm to the environment, to taonga species, and to tikanga Māori.
c: Press release reintroducing her member's bill to ban seabed mining, after the fast-track panel rejected Trans-Tasman Resources' application
s: Te Pāti Māori release via Scoop

q: Protecting our moana and standing with coastal iwi and hapū is why I got into politics in the first place. This Bill is about finishing what we started and making sure these protections are finally locked in for future generations.
c: Same seabed-mining release
s: Te Pāti Māori release via Scoop

q: You give your candidate vote to Aperehama, [and] Willow-Jean Prime - who is at seven on her party list - and Huhana Lyndon - who is also on seven on her party list - you get three... and so on and so forth, and that's how you work it out.

q: suggestion is not ours to make
c: Asked by media which party Māori voters should give their party vote to

q: This list proves we are putting our money where our mouth is.

q: I can hear the anger and feel the pain.

q: If I have done you wrong, I offer you my head.

q: He was the reason why I was inspired to come into politics.

q: you're going up against the 115 people who are against you
c: Describing debating in Parliament, same TVNZ interview

q: I think you have this really naive energy engine room in your soul when you're so young, you think you can solve all the world's problems, especially when you've got a grandfather and grandparents like mine, and you just use that energy while you can.
c: Same TVNZ interview

q: Iwi and hapuu voices matter. Decisions about our whenua and communities must be made with the people who whakapapa to those places.
c: Statement on Waikato and Waipā river commitments

q: We call on the Government to honour its commitments and enter into a new era of co-management and co-governance with Waikato-Tainui, as set out in the Waikato-Tainui Raupatu Claims (Waikato River) Settlement Act 2010.
c: Same statement

q: I confirm that the comments claiming to be mine are not. I did not and have not spoken with any reporter on this matter.

q: committed member of Te Pāti Māori, committed to Tāmaki Makaurau, and committed to making this a one term government.

q: All our policies have been designed by Māori for Māori to Māori, and it really does give weight to, and rise to, the fact that what's good for Māori is good for all of Aotearoa.
c: Same debate, on the party's tax policy

q: There's no more emergency housing to catch those who are homeless at the moment, we're just moving them on, round and round in circles, creating more deprivation, punching down on the pōhara instead of creating real viable solutions.

q: It's not untoward where political parties have dissension and difficulty. It's a matter of growing through that, and it's where we are at the moment.
c: Interview with Te Ao Māori News on party turmoil
